articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the issuance of an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026.
This amendment modifies existing authorizations concerning transactions involving Iran, though specific details of the changes were not immediately released by OFAC.

Such general licenses are often issued to clarify or expand permissible activities under sanctions programs, aiming to minimize unintended humanitarian or economic impacts while maintaining pressure on the sanctioned regime.

These actions aim to counter illicit activities and human rights abuses associated with these regimes.

The specific individuals or entities designated, and the nature of their illicit activities, were not detailed in the initial announcement but typically involve proliferation financing, cybercrime, or corruption.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking and Rejecting Transactions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on October 26, 2026, regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC.
These amendments aim to provide updated guidance and clarity for financial institutions and other entities on their obligations under U.S. sanctions programs.
The updated FAQs are crucial for ensuring proper compliance procedures and understanding reporting requirements to OFAC.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran, Russia General Licenses; Removes Belarus, North Korea Designations
body: On October 21, 2026, OFAC announced new Iran-related designations and issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses.
Concurrently, OFAC also announced the removal of certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea, indicating a recalibration of sanctions measures.
Additionally, amended Frequently Asked Questions were issued to provide further guidance on these changes, reflecting ongoing adjustments to U.S. foreign policy objectives.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities Under Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA)
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026, along with the issuance of associated General Licenses.
These designations target entities involved in the theft of American intellectual property, a key focus of U.S. national security and economic policy.

The action follows previous sanctions against five entities connected to Chinese national Linwei Ding, founder of Shanghai Zhisuan Technology Co. Ltd., for alleged significant theft of trade secrets of United States persons.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: On October 16, 2026, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question.
These updates aim to provide clarity and potentially adjust the scope of permissible activities under the Venezuela sanctions program.
Such amendments often reflect ongoing diplomatic efforts or changes in the humanitarian situation within Venezuela.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related and Cuba Entities; Issues New General Licenses

Concurrently, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions to provide guidance on these actions.
These measures are part of ongoing efforts to address threats posed by these regimes and to refine the implementation of U.S. sanctions policies.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: On October 14, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation.
Such removals can signify a change in the designated entity's behavior, a shift in U.S. policy, or successful diplomatic engagement.
This action may ease certain restrictions related to the previously designated entity.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations

These designations target individuals and entities involved in illicit drug trafficking and terrorist financing networks globally.
The actions underscore the U.S. government's commitment to disrupting these criminal and terrorist organizations and protecting the international financial system.

articles.headline: U.S. Adds Three Chinese Biomedical Companies to UFLPA Entity List
body: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced the addition of three Chinese biomedical technology companies to the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA) Entity List, effective October 29, 2026.

These companies, identified as Shenzhen BGI Technology Co., Ltd. (BGI Group), BGI Genomics Co., Ltd., and MGI Tech Co., Ltd., are accused of working with the government of the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region to recruit, transport, transfer, harbor, or receive forced labor or members of persecuted groups out of Xinjiang.

China's Ministry of Commerce has strongly condemned the decision, asserting that the U.S. is using human rights concerns as a pretext to restrict Chinese businesses and that the allegations of forced labor in Xinjiang are baseless.
articles.source: Department of Homeland Security / Federal Register / Reuters

articles.headline: USTR Proposes Two-Month Extension for Section 301 Maritime Actions Suspension Against China
body: The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) has proposed a two-month extension, through January 9, 2027, for the suspension of Section 301 responsive actions against China's maritime, logistics, and shipbuilding sectors.
This extension aims to allow for further negotiations with China on the issues raised in the investigation.

The current one-year suspension, part of a broader U.S.-China trade and economic deal, was set to expire on November 9, 2026, and without further action, port fees on maritime transport services and related duties would resume.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Significant Enforcement Actions Against American Express National Bank and Bank of America
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released its enforcement actions for October 2026, including substantial penalties against American Express National Bank and Bank of America, National Association.

American Express National Bank, Sandy, Utah, was issued a Cease and Desist Order and a $350 million civil money penalty for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and violations related to customer due diligence and customer identification programs.

Bank of America, National Association, Charlotte, North Carolina, also faced a $750 million civil money penalty for similar BSA compliance program deficiencies, untimely suspicious activity report filings, and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information.

Similarly, Christopher Organista, a Former Operations Processor at the La Mirada, California Operations Center of U.S. Bank National Association, Cincinnati, Ohio, received a prohibition order for embezzling approximately $194,131 in bank customer funds.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
